name: NWOBHM
about: The New Wave of British Heavy Metal was the name Sounds gave in 1979 to a surge of young bands who had learned from Sabbath, Priest and UFO but absorbed punk's speed, independence and do-it-yourself singles. Centred on London's Soundhouse, the North East and the Midlands, it was fast, melodic and built for gang vocals, with twin guitars, galloping bass and a working-class swagger; the first records were self-released seven-inches and the Metal for Muthas compilation. Iron Maiden, Saxon and Def Leppard became stars, Diamond Head's riffs were later mined by Metallica, and Venom and Witchfinder General pointed toward black metal and doom. By 1983 the wave had crested, but thrash, power metal and almost everything since descends from it.

artists.name: Iron Maiden
artists.why: the movement's biggest and most enduring band

artists.name: Def Leppard
artists.why: Sheffield teenagers who went to America

artists.name: Judas Priest
artists.why: veterans who set the pace in 1980

artists.name: Venom
artists.why: the ugly end that became black metal

artists.name: Satan
artists.why: Newcastle's most technical and most revived

albums.title: Overkill
albums.why: The double-bass-drum title track and Lemmy's growl arrived a year before the wave broke, and every young band in it took its cue from here.

albums.title: British Steel
albums.why: The old guard's answer to the new bands: short, hard, chant-ready songs like Breaking the Law and Living After Midnight that set the NWOBHM's commercial template.

albums.title: Iron Maiden
albums.why: Paul Di'Anno's punkish snarl, Steve Harris's bass and Phantom of the Opera on a rough debut that nevertheless defined the movement's sound.

albums.title: Wheels of Steel
albums.why: 747 (Strangers in the Night) and the title track gave Saxon their hits and the NWOBHM its biker anthems; direct, unpretentious and still played.

albums.title: Strong Arm of the Law
albums.why: Released seven months after Wheels of Steel, it is the tighter and faster of the pair and the Saxon record thrash bands point to.

albums.title: Lightning to the Nations
albums.why: Self-released in a white sleeve, with Am I Evil? and Helpless, the record Lars Ulrich studied and the most inventive riff-writing the movement produced.

albums.title: Angel Witch
albums.why: Kevin Heybourne's occult melodies and the title track's chorus make this the cult NWOBHM album, a line straight from Sabbath to Mercyful Fate.

albums.title: Ace of Spades
albums.why: Not strictly of the wave but its godfather record, with the title song and (We Are) The Road Crew at the peak of the Lemmy, Clarke and Taylor line-up.

albums.title: Metal for Muthas
albums.why: EMI's cash-in compilation gave Iron Maiden, Samson, Praying Mantis and Angel Witch their first wide hearing; uneven, but a document of the scene's birth.

albums.title: On Through the Night
albums.why: The Sheffield teenagers' debut is thin and overproduced in places, but Wasted and Rock Brigade show the arena ambition that would soon leave the scene behind.

albums.title: Head On
albums.why: Bruce Dickinson's recorded debut, as Bruce Bruce, fronting Paul Samson's bluesier metal; worth hearing for the voice that Maiden would hire.

albums.title: Hit and Run
albums.why: Kim McAuliffe and Kelly Johnson's band at their best, with the title track and a Motörhead-adjacent rush that earned them a tour and a joint single with Lemmy.

albums.title: Spellbound
albums.why: John Sykes on guitar and Jon Deverill's vocals lifted the Tygers from the pack; Gangland and the title track are the melodic end of the wave at its best.

albums.title: Rock Until You Drop
albums.why: The Gallagher brothers' athletic rock was faster than almost anything else in 1981, and Metallica took Raven on their first American tour for a reason.

albums.title: Welcome to Hell
albums.why: Cronos, Mantas and Abaddon's debut is incompetent and hugely important in equal measure, the Satanic noise from which thrash and black metal grew.

albums.title: Night of the Demon
albums.why: Dave Hill's horror-themed band made more melodic music than the sleeve suggests, and the title song and Don't Break the Circle are NWOBHM standards.

albums.title: The Nightcomers
albums.why: Edinburgh's Holocaust wrote Death or Glory, which Metallica later covered, on a dark, heavy album that stands out from the wave's more upbeat records.

albums.title: High 'n' Dry
albums.why: Mutt Lange's first Leppard production sharpened the songs and the sound, and Bringin' On the Heartbreak signalled where they were headed.

albums.title: The Number of the Beast
albums.why: Bruce Dickinson's arrival and Run to the Hills took Maiden to number one, the point where the NWOBHM stopped being a scene and became the mainstream of metal.

albums.title: Death Penalty
albums.why: Stourbridge's Sabbath disciples slowed the wave to a doom crawl with a sleeve that caused a tabloid fuss; a founding record of traditional doom.

albums.title: Filth Hounds of Hades
albums.why: Algy Ward, ex-Damned, led a trio that played like Motörhead's younger brothers, produced by Fast Eddie Clarke and loved by thrash's first generation.

albums.title: Court in the Act
albums.why: Late in the wave, Newcastle's Satan made its most technical album, with Trial by Fire and Break Free prefiguring thrash and speed metal.

albums.title: A Time of Changes
albums.why: Released after the band had split and reformed, it finally put the Metallica-covered title song on an album, alongside solid, if late, NWOBHM standards.

albums.title: Life Sentence
albums.why: The classic line-up's reunion album picks up where Court in the Act left off, the best record of the NWOBHM revival that followed the 2000s.
